As explained there, the geographic extent of the 203(b)(8) exemption relates to a municipality and the adjacent area which is commercially integrated with that municipality. That area may include other distinct cities, for there is no requirement of mutual exclusivity - that is, a city with its own commercial zone may also be included in the commercial zone of another 14 city.
Since the utility of defining commercial zones according to catchwords such as "intercity," "intercommunity," 15 "intraterminal," and "single community" has diminished as the clear and ascertainable meaning of these terms has dimmed,
The Commission discussed this issue in relation to New York City and Newark, N.J., in an earlier decision, stating:
More important than such considerations as distance, terminals, equipment, and the use of city streets is the nature and development of the area involved. As urged by opponents of an enlarged New York City zone it is, no doubt, true that Newark and possibly some of the other New Jersey municipalities here involved began their development on the days of slower and less effective transportation as municipalities apart from and in competition with New York City. Traditionally, they have tended to keep their independence and no doubt the competition between them has intensified but even these considerations are not controlling. Adjacent, even contiguous, municipalities are generally vigorously independent and competitive for industries which supply equipment and directly and indirectly provide tax sources, but it is not difficult to cite a number of such which are unquestionably within the same commercial zone for the purposes of section 203(b)(8). ... Clearly the traditional independence and competition between New York City and New Jersey municipalities such as Newark does not preclude a finding that transportation between them is now essentially local or intraterminal in character and confined to a commercial zone which may be said to be based on New York City.

In Freight Forwarders Institute v. United States, the three-judge court described the phrase "single community homogeneity" as a "fast-fading concept," 409 F. Supp. at 704. Earlier in the discussion the court stated: "A study of the Commission's report and order, as well as previous decisions of the Commission relating to the size of terminal areas and commercial zones, reveals a perplexing montage constructed through the use of seemingly interchangeable terms such as 'intracity movement,' 'intracommunity movement,' 'local transportation,' and 'movement within a commercial zone.' The strongly divergent positions of the parties as to the specific ground for the Commission's decision now under review appear to stem from the use of these various terms." 409 F. Supp. at 700.
